summary.headline: Sri Lanka's strongest private bank, priced close to fair value: Rs 211 against a Rs 214 fair value; rebuilt from the reports
summary.text: Commercial Bank of Ceylon (COMB.N0000 voting, COMB.X0000 non-voting) is the country's largest private bank: Rs 3.87tn of assets, Rs 2.43tn of loans, branches in Bangladesh and a bank in the Maldives. This full rebuild re-read the four CSE reports. Nine-month group profit rose 9% to Rs 52.2bn (EPS Rs 31.08), loans grew 17% in nine months, and gross Stage 3 loans fell to 5.31%, but provisions (Rs 16.6bn, +18%) and costs (+20%) grew faster than income (+14%). At Rs 211.00 (CSE, 27 November 2026) the voting share trades at 0.94x group NAV of Rs 224.63, 5.4x trailing earnings and a 5.0% dividend yield. Fair value is about Rs 214, up from Rs 182 because book value has grown, 2027 earnings look higher, and the dividend model now follows Damodaran's two-stage form. Buy up to Rs 182; Rs 161 or less is a strong buy. The voting share hasn't traded that low in 2026 (low Rs 189); the non-voting share, with the same dividends, is Rs 189, only 4% above the buy price. Watch capital (CET1 12.5%, total capital 16.35% against a 14% minimum), impairments as the new loans season, and a provisional beta. Management misses its own goals of ROE over 20% and profit growth over 20%.

tests.label: Net debt no more than equity
tests.note: A bank, so judged on capital: CET1 12.50% (minimum 8.5%), total capital 16.35% (minimum 14%), leverage ratio 7.58% (minimum 3%). Headroom on total capital is 2.35 points after 17% loan growth in nine months; Rs 20bn of Tier 2 debentures raised in July 2026.

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.note: Profit in each of the ten years to 2025, including the 2022 crisis; 2023 was the low point (bank ROE 9.8%). 2024 included a Rs 62.8bn impairment reversal and a Rs 41.0bn loss on the debt exchange.

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends

requiredReturn.betaBasis: Provisional. A bank, so the sector's levered beta is used without relevering: Damodaran's January 2026 Bank (Money Center) 0.70 (web-search extract, as for SAMP, HNB and NDB), against a median local beta of 0.97 (StockAnalysis 0.69 five-year, TradingView 1.06, Simply Wall St 0.97; the last two don't state their window). The higher, 0.97, is used. Refresh in January 2027.

requiredReturn.note: Cost of equity = 8.24% + 0.97 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 18.2%; bear +1.5, bull −1.5 points. No WACC: a bank is valued on equity (P/B, P/E, dividends, residual income). With the 5-year StockAnalysis beta alone (so 0.70 from Damodaran) the cost of equity would be about 15.4% and fair value much higher.

highlights.title: Nine months to September 2026 (group, unaudited)
highlights.text: Profit after tax up 8.6% to Rs 52.2bn; EPS Rs 31.08 against Rs 29.05. Gross income up 18.9% to Rs 318.8bn and net interest income up 17.0% to Rs 121.1bn; pre-tax profit up 8.7% to Rs 79.7bn.

highlights.title: The third quarter
highlights.text: Profit Rs 16.7bn, down 0.7% on a year earlier (EPS Rs 9.95 against Rs 10.18): a Rs 2.0bn trading loss replaced last year's Rs 2.2bn gain, and costs rose 23%. Impairment eased to Rs 1.7bn after Rs 11.7bn in the June quarter.

highlights.title: Costs, provisions and taxes
highlights.text: Operating expenses up 19.9% (staff, technology); impairment Rs 16.6bn (+17.8%), set aside for 'external pressures on local businesses'; taxes on financial services up 25.4% to Rs 16.8bn. Bank cost-to-income 40.0% including those taxes (39.2% for 2025).

highlights.title: Loans, deposits and asset quality
highlights.text: Gross loans up Rs 348bn (16.7%) to Rs 2.43tn in nine months, 27.6% in a year; deposits up 15.5% to Rs 3.12tn. Gross Stage 3 5.31% (5.81% in December), net 1.47%, coverage 72.35%. Margin 4.45% (4.51%) as deposit costs rose.

highlights.title: Capital
highlights.text: Bank CET1 12.50% (13.04% in December) and total capital 16.35% (16.70%), against minimums of 8.5% and 14%; third-quarter profit isn't yet counted. Rs 20bn of Tier 2 debentures raised in July. Fitch upgraded the national rating to AA(lka) in October.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: (Long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth) × NAV Rs 224.63: 0.68x / 0.90x / 1.24x book, with ROE 15% / 17% / 19% and growth 5% / 6% / 7%. The price implies a long-run ROE of about 17.4%.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: 2027 group EPS Rs 40 / 45 / 49 × 4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5. Base is 5% above the Rs 42.92 run-rate (Q1 2026 × 4) and 16% above trailing Rs 38.89; the P/Es are within the bank's 2021–2025 range and at or below the justified 4.8x / 5.6x / 7.0x.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Next year's dividend Rs 11.0 / 12.5 / 14.0 (about 28% of 2027 EPS, as for 2025, counting the share part), growing 7% / 10% / 12% for five years (below the 14% supported), then 5% / 6% / 7% with the payout rising to 1 − growth ÷ ROE (63–67%), at the cost of equity.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Used instead of a cash-flow DCF, which doesn't suit a bank. Book Rs 224.63 plus profit above the cost of equity: ROE moves in a straight line from 18.6% (trailing) to 15% / 17% / 19% over ten years, 28% payout, then the excess return grows at 5% / 6% / 7%.

modelsNote: A bank's cash flows are mostly lending and deposits, so instead of a cash-flow DCF I used residual income and a justified price-to-book, with P/E and dividends, all at the 18.2% cost of equity (19.7% / 16.7% bear / bull) and all worked by scripts/valuation.py. Growth check: assumed 7% / 10% / 12% a year for the next five years against 14.0% supported (71.5% of profit kept × 19.6% ROE); all within 2 points. Long-run growth 5–7% stays below the 12.24% bond yield and needs 26–37% of profit kept. The four methods agree closely in the base case (Rs 202–248).

assumptions.label: Profit and dividend growth, next five years

scenarios.common: Cost of equity from the house formula (risk-free 8.24% + beta 0.97 × 10.28% equity premium). Payout about 28% of EPS including the share dividend. Shares 1,654.5m (1,557.1m voting + 97.3m non-voting); the share dividend and ESOPs add about 1–2% a year.

sensitivity.title: Residual income base case, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Each 1.5 points on the cost of equity moves the base value by about Rs 32–43 a share, so the provisional beta matters more than next year's profit. Today's Rs 211 sits between the base and the bull column at the base cost of equity.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 86,050 in total, against Rs 105,500 for 500 voting shares at Rs 211. The non-voting share (COMB.X0000, Rs 189, same dividends, no vote) reaches the first tier after a 4% fall and is the more practical way in.
buyPlan.realism: For the voting share, Rs 182 needs a 14% fall and is below the 2026 low of Rs 189 (January–March); it last traded there in 2025 (July–September low Rs 156.50). The lower tiers need a sharp market or bank-specific setback. The non-voting share traded at Rs 178 in January–March 2026, so its first two tiers are within this year's range.

Lower interest rates, which would lower the cost of equity and lift bond values.

New taxes on banks, or higher taxes on financial services (already up 25%).
Stress in Bangladesh or the Maldives, or in the government-bond market.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the 2025 annual report and the 2026 interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, the beta is provisional, and the price is the CSE close of 27 November 2026, so check it before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

Decision box.Verdict: Watch list: Rs 211 is about 1% below fair value of Rs 214 but 16% above the Rs 182 buy price.
Decision box.Expected yearly return at Rs 211: About 17–18% a year if the price stays near 0.94x book: dividend 5.0% plus book growth of about 13%. That is close to the 18.2% cost of equity, so little margin.
Decision box.Downside / upside: Bear case Rs 154 (−27%); bull case Rs 300 (+42%).
Decision box.What the price assumes: At 0.94x NAV, with 6% long-run growth and an 18.2% cost of equity, a long-run ROE of about 17.4%, near the base case.
Decision box.Confidence: Medium: the four methods agree (Rs 202–248 base), but the beta is provisional and impairments are rising.
Decision box.Margin of safety: Not yet for the voting share; the non-voting share is 4% above the buy price.

Business and moat.What it does: Sri Lanka's largest private-sector bank: 295 branches, Rs 2.36tn of bank loans and Rs 3.0tn of deposits (September 2026), 21 branches in Bangladesh, a majority-owned bank in the Maldives, CBC Finance (leasing) and a representative office in Dubai.
Business and moat.Moat: Moderate: scale, the largest SME lender (30.3% of SME loans among 16 banks), a 37% CASA ratio and a strong brand; but banking is regulated and competitive.
Business and moat.Growth: Loans grew 36% in 2025 and 17% more in nine months of 2026; capital, not demand, is the limit.

Accounting quality.Underlying earnings: 2025 profit is clean of the 2024 debt-restructuring effects (a Rs 62.8bn impairment reversal and Rs 41.0bn derecognition loss in 2024).
Accounting quality.One-offs: 2026 trading gains were Rs 2.9bn for nine months but a Rs 2.0bn loss in Q3; bond-sale gains fell to Rs 0.7bn from Rs 2.6bn.
Accounting quality.Dividends in shares: Part of each dividend since 2022 is paid in new shares (Rs 2.50 of Rs 10.50 for 2025), which keeps capital in the bank but adds about 1% more shares a year.

Sri Lanka checks.Interest rates: Watch: rising deposit costs cut the margin to 4.45%; FVOCI bond losses of Rs 2.3bn went through equity in nine months.
Sri Lanka checks.Rupee: Watch: a quarter of loans and deposits are in foreign currency; translation gains of Rs 4.1bn in nine months went to equity.
Sri Lanka checks.Tax and regulation: Risk: taxes on financial services (Rs 16.8bn, +25%) plus income tax take over 40% of pre-tax operating profit.
Sri Lanka checks.Dependence on the state: Watch: about Rs 1.0tn of government and other debt securities (amortised cost and FVOCI).

Investment case and sell rules.Why own it: The country's best-capitalised private bank with ROE near 19%, falling bad loans and a steady dividend, at just below book value.
Investment case and sell rules.The case is broken if: ROE falls below 15% for a full year, gross Stage 3 rises back above 7%, or capital forces a rights issue at a low price.
Investment case and sell rules.Sell triggers: Price more than 30% above fair value (above Rs 280); the case breaks; or a clearly better opportunity appears.

Suggested Telegram alerts (not set; need.Buy: Rs 182 or lower (voting); non-voting COMB.X0000 also at Rs 182 or lower

What this analysis doesn't cover: Damodaran's sector-beta pages and the local beta pages couldn't be opened in this run; the beta of 0.97 rests on web-search extracts, and only one source (0.69) states a 5-year window. Recheck in January 2027.
Bangladesh and Maldives results weren't analysed separately (segment 'International operations' made Rs 14.8bn of segment result in nine months, down from Rs 23.8bn).
Commercial Bank gives no profit guidance for 2026–2027; the EPS cases are my assumptions.
Peer banks (SAMP, HNB) weren't compared in this run.
Shareholder figures cover the voting shares; the non-voting top 20 are mostly individuals (Akbar Brothers largest at 7.30%).

fullText:
**Commercial Bank of Ceylon (COMB.N0000 / COMB.X0000): full rebuild, 27 November 2026**

**Summary.** Sri Lanka's largest private bank is a good business at close to a fair price. At Rs 211.00 the voting share is 0.94x group NAV (Rs 224.63), 5.4x trailing EPS (Rs 38.89) and yields 5.0%. Fair value is about Rs 214; buy up to Rs 182, strong buy at Rs 161 or less. Business tests 4 of 4: category 2, watch list (unchanged).

**What changed since 12 November.** This is a full rebuild from the four CSE reports, with the research record now holding only printed figures. Fair value moves from Rs 182 to Rs 214 because (1) NAV rose from Rs 216.14 (June) to Rs 224.63 (September); (2) 2027 EPS assumptions rise to Rs 40 / 45 / 49 on the nine-month results; (3) the cost of equity now comes from the house formula (beta 0.97, provisional), 18.2% base, almost the same as the 18% used before; and (4) the dividend model now follows Damodaran's two-stage form, in which the payout rises to 1 − growth ÷ ROE after five years. Before, it kept a 29% payout forever and gave only Rs 99, far below the other methods.

**Results.** Nine months to September 2026: group profit Rs 52.2bn (+8.6%), EPS Rs 31.08 (+7%). Net interest income +17%, fees +16%, but impairment +18% (Rs 16.6bn, mostly a Q2 buffer), costs +20% and taxes on financial services +25%. The third quarter was flat (−0.7%) after a trading loss. Gross loans +17% in nine months (+28% in a year); gross Stage 3 down to 5.31%.

**Valuation (Rs a share, bear / base / bull).**
- Justified P/B: 152.8 / 202.5 / 277.9
- P/E (2027 EPS × P/E): 180.0 / 247.5 / 318.5
- Dividend model: 138.8 / 206.6 / 303.5
- Residual income: 146.3 / 204.4 / 301.3
- Averages 154.5 / 215.3 / 300.3, weighted 30/50/20 = Rs 214.03. Buy (−15%) Rs 181.92; strong buy (−25%) Rs 160.52.

**Assumptions.** Cost of equity 19.7% / 18.2% / 16.7% (risk-free 8.24% + 0.97 × 10.28%). Long-run ROE 15% / 17% / 19%; long-run growth 5% / 6% / 7% (below the 12.24% bond yield). Growth for five years 7% / 10% / 12% against 14.0% supported (71.5% of profit kept × 19.6% ROE). Base 2027 EPS is 5% above the Rs 42.92 run-rate. The price implies a long-run ROE of about 17.4%.

**Management.** The 2025 report promises disciplined growth in productive sectors, OneApp in 2026, a McKinsey retail programme, more overseas profit and Rs 100bn of green loans by 2030. Delivered: Rs 20bn of Tier 2 debentures raised; capital still above minimums; bad loans falling. Missed: the bank's own goals of ROE over 20% (19.5% in 2025, 19.3% in 2026 so far) and profit growth over 20% (8% and 8%).

**Shareholders.** No controlling owner. Mr Y S H I Silva, Mr D P Pieris, DFCC Bank, the EPF and the IFC (with two funds) are the largest voting holders; 99.82% is public. The only big move in the September quarter was a transfer between Sri Lanka Insurance accounts.

**Buy plan (500 shares).** 200 at up to Rs 182, 150 at Rs 171, 150 at Rs 160: about Rs 86,050 in total, average Rs 172. The voting share hasn't traded below Rs 189 in 2026, so this needs a 14% fall. The non-voting share (Rs 189, same dividends, no vote) is only 4% above the buy price and traded at Rs 178 in January–March; it is the practical way to buy.

**Risks.** Provisions as the fast loan growth seasons; capital headroom (total capital 16.35% against 14%); deposit costs squeezing the margin; taxes on banks; overseas operations; and a provisional beta: each 1.5 points on the cost of equity moves fair value by about Rs 30–40.

This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
